title: Cicatrizing Conjunctivitis: The Definitive Visual Guide to Progressive Ocular Scarring
summary: A comprehensive clinical breakdown of rare, bilateral, sight-threatening conjunctival disorders characterized by inflammation, goblet cell loss, and progressive scarring. Early diagnosis and expert intervention are essential to prevent ocular surface failure and blinding keratopathy.

sections.title: Disease Hallmarks & Critical Warnings
content: Cicatrizing conjunctivitis: rare, usually bilateral, sight-threatening group of disorders.
Hallmarks: loss of goblet cells, ocular surface failure (from chronic limbitis, limbal epithelial stem cell (lesC) failure | blinding keratopathy), and progressive conjunctival scarring.
Onset may be insidious, delaying diagnosis.
CRITICAL: Get expert help early—it is very easy to underestimate these conditions.

sections.title: Pattern Key
sections.content: ssP, static or slowly progressive; Prog, progressive. (Page 412, 214, Chapter 6 Conjunctiva)

branches: Chronic inflammatory subepithelial blistering disease of mucous membranes
Age: >60y usually; may occur in adolescents (more severe disease)
Markers: Linear deposition of Ig and complement at BM zone of mucosal surfaces
Targets: Antibodies specific to components of BM and hemidesmosomes (triggers unclear)
Associations: Rheumatoid arthritis (rA) and pernicious anaemia
Locations: Oral mucosa and conjunctiva (most common); skin and other membranes; Trachea/Oesophagus (life-threatening)

sections.title: MMP: Diagnosis & Clinical Features
content: International Consensus Diagnosis: Requires direct immunopathological confirmation + typical clinical features.
OcMMP Specific Diagnosis: Primarily clinical; immunopathology provides supporting evidence only.
Symptom: Irritation.
Conjunctival Signs: Acute/chronic papillary conjunctivitis, subconjunctival bulla ± ulceration.
Progressive Cicatrization: Loss of plica semilunaris and fornices, symblepharon/ankyloblepharon formation.
Lid/Surface Signs: Trichiasis, cicatricial entropion, dry eye, 2° microbial keratitis, corneal neovascularization, ulcerative keratitis, perforation, lesC failure, keratinization.

sections.title: MMP Treatment Strategy
content: 1. Early Diagnosis & Specialist Referral: Refer early for help to improve outcome.
2. Adnexa Management: Ensure lids/lashes don't cause inflammation; use early conjunctiva-sparing surgery.
3. Maximize Tear Film: Punctal occlusion, tear substitutes; treat MgD and blepharitis.
4. Exclude Infection: Must rule out infection before attributing inflammation to disease; risk factors include poor surface and lid trauma.
5. Define Residual Inflammation: Any inflammation remaining after 2° causes are treated is disease-related.

rows: Use with caution; may mask disease.
'Step-down strategy'; continuous dosing/taper or IV pulses.

sections.title: MMP Management Notes & Complications
content: Immunosuppression generally required for >1y.
NB: Clinically quiescent eyes may have occult inflammation resulting in progression.
Monitoring: Photography and measurements (e.g., fornix depth measurer).
Surgery: Entropion/trichiasis repair, oral mucosal grafting for fornix reconstruction.
Corneal Issues: Persistent epithelial defects, lesC failure, perforations.
Mechanical: Botulinum toxin (limited use due to restriction but can be effective).
End-stage: May require osteo-odonto-keratoprosthesis.

branches: Acute, severe dermatosis: epidermal loss + multisite mucositis + systemic disturbance
Incidence: 1–2 cases per million per year
Initiators: Drugs (sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol) or Infection (Mycoplasma, HSV)
Pathophysiology: MHC Class I drug presentation -> CD8+ CTL expansion -> Granulysin mediator
Molecules: TNF-α, interferon (IFN), inducible nitric oxide synthase
Prognosis: Systemic disease severity predictors do NOT predict acute or chronic ocular disease

sections.title: SCORTEN Parameters
content: Age >40y
Presence of malignancy
Heart rate >120 bpm
Epidermal detachment >10% BSA at admission
Serum urea >10mmol
Serum glucose >14mmol
Bicarbonate <20mmol

sections.title: SJS/TEN Ocular Classification
content: Mild: Eyelid oedema, mild conjunctival injection, chemosis.
Moderate: Membranous conjunctivitis ± corneal epithelial defects (>30% healing with med therapy) ± corneal ulceration ± corneal infiltrates.
Severe: Symblepharon formation ± non-healing corneal epithelial defects ± visual loss ± conjunctival fornix foreshortening (as for OcMMP).

sections.title: SJS/TEN Acute Ocular Treatment
content: Multidisciplinary care; regional burns unit preferred.
Lubricant: Non-preserved hyaluronate/carmellose every 2h.
Hygiene: Daily by ophthalmologist/trained nurse.
Corticosteroids: Non-preserved dexamethasone 0.1% 2×/d.
Antibiotics: Broad-spectrum (e.g., moxifloxacin 4×/d) if staining/ulceration present.
Exposure Prevention: Essential in unconscious patients.
Surgery: Adhesion division; symblepharon rings (controversial); gas-permeable scleral Cl; conformers.
Amniotic Membrane Grafting (AMG): To protect surfaces/lids (John’s procedure); ProKera®; Omnilenz™; amnion-wrapped conformer ± subtarsal triamcinolone 20mg.

sections.title: SJS/TEN Systemic & Chronic Phases
sections.content: Systemic Immunosuppression: Controversy surrounds systemic steroids (role in ocular disease vs negative systemic effect). Usually given for acute scleritis. Possible role for IVIG and IV ciclosporin. Chronic Phase: Sequelae include persistent inflammation, scleritis, ocular surface failure, and cicatrizing changes with OcMMP phenotype. Management follows OcMMP or scleritis protocols. Progression can occur years after acute illness.

rows: Thermal, radiation, chemical (alkali), surgical (e.g., glaucoma surgery).
Anterior (Staphylococcal): limited cicatrization/keratinization of lid margin.
Most common with C. trachomatis; also membranous/pseudomembranous conjunctivitis.
Ectodermal dysplasia (hair/teeth abnormalities); Epidermolysis bullosa (hemidesmosome disease).
Unilateral: sebaceous cell carcinoma, conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia, or SCC; lymphoma.

sections.title: Drug-Induced Cicatrization
content: Clinically indistinguishable from OcMMP.
Systemic: Practolol (discontinued), penicillamine.
Topical: Propine (discontinued), pilocarpine, timolol, idoxuridine, gentamicin (especially 1.5%), guanethidine.

branches: Occurs in allogeneic bone marrow transplant (donor leucocytes attack recipient)
Acute Response: TEN-like response; pseudomembranous conjunctivitis
Chronic Response: Scleroderma-like skin changes; Sjögren’s-like gland changes
Posterior Segment (Rare): Posterior scleritis, choroidal thickening during acute stage

rows: Pseudomembranous conjunctivitis with corneal epithelial sloughing
